headline: Capcom Looks Toward a Future of Making Video Games With AI's Help

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Capcom is a big company that makes video games, like Resident Evil. Making a huge game takes a lot of work. Even small jobs, like fixing tiny details, can take a long time. A Capcom worker named Satoshi Ishida talked about this problem at a special meeting. He said the company wants to use AI to help make games faster. AI is computer technology that can learn and do tasks almost like a person. Capcom uses a special tool called RE Engine to build its games. Ishida said Capcom wants to slowly turn this tool into one that uses more AI help. But Capcom says it will not let AI create the actual art or characters in its games. Instead, AI will just help workers do their jobs quicker. Ishida said someday, people and AI might work together to make games. This shows how AI is starting to change many jobs, even fun ones like making video games.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Capcom, the company behind games like Resident Evil, is thinking hard about how AI could change the way games get made. A programmer named Satoshi Ishida gave a talk explaining that building huge games is extremely hard work. Even simple tasks can take a surprising amount of time when a game is as big and detailed as Resident Evil. Ishida explained that one answer to this problem is using AI more smartly during the development process, which is all the behind-the-scenes work of coding, designing, and testing a game. Capcom has already said it won't let AI generate things like character designs or artwork for its games. Instead, the company wants AI to help speed up the boring or repetitive parts of game-making, so human developers can focus on creative decisions. Ishida talked about slowly changing Capcom's game-building software, called RE Engine, into a tool built around AI assistance. His long-term goal is a future where humans and AI work side by side to create games together. This idea matters because it shows a balance companies are trying to find: using AI to save time and money, while still keeping humans in charge of the creative parts. As AI tools get more powerful, more industries, not just video games, may face similar questions about where AI should help and where it shouldn't.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Capcom, the Japanese company famous for franchises like Resident Evil, is rethinking how it builds games by relying more on artificial intelligence. During a presentation at a company event, programmer Satoshi Ishida explained a problem many big game studios face: as games get more detailed and realistic, even small, routine tasks during development can eat up enormous amounts of time. His proposed fix is integrating AI tools into the development workflow, meaning the step-by-step process developers use to code, design, test, and polish a game before it's released. Importantly, Capcom has publicly stated it will not use AI to generate finished game assets, such as artwork, characters, or music, that players actually see or hear. Instead, the company wants AI to act more like a behind-the-scenes assistant, handling repetitive or time-consuming tasks so human developers can spend more time on creative decisions. Ishida described a gradual plan to transform Capcom's in-house game-building software, called RE Engine, into what he called an 'AI-generation game engine.' His ultimate vision, as translated by gaming outlet IGN, is a future where people and AI create games together as collaborators rather than AI simply replacing human creativity. This story matters because it reflects a bigger debate happening across many industries right now: how much should companies rely on AI, and where should the line be drawn between using AI as a helpful tool versus letting it take over creative or artistic work? Capcom's stance tries to find a middle ground, using AI for efficiency while still insisting that humans remain the creative decision-makers. As AI technology keeps improving, more companies in entertainment, software, and beyond will likely face similar choices, and how they answer could shape job opportunities and the kinds of games, movies, or products we see in the future.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: Capcom, the studio behind major franchises like Resident Evil, is signaling a significant shift in how it plans to develop games going forward, one that leans heavily on artificial intelligence, though not in the way some might assume. At a recent event called the Capcom Open Conference RE: 2026, programmer Satoshi Ishida delivered a presentation outlining the operational challenges of producing games at Resident Evil's scale. He noted that as games grow more complex and visually detailed, even minor, routine development tasks can become extremely time-consuming for human teams. His proposed solution centers on what he called successfully integrating AI technology into development workflows, essentially using AI as a tool to streamline the technical and repetitive aspects of game-building rather than the creative ones. This distinction is important because Capcom has previously stated publicly that it will not use AI-generated assets, meaning it won't let AI create finished artwork, character models, or other content that players directly experience in the final game. Ishida's comments appear consistent with that policy, framing AI's role as a productivity booster rather than a creative replacement. Still, his remarks leave room for AI's role to expand over time. He described a gradual, incremental plan to transform Capcom's proprietary game engine, RE Engine (the core software that developers use to build and run their games), into what he termed an 'AI-generation game engine.' According to a translation by IGN, Ishida's broader vision points toward 'a future where we create games together with AI,' suggesting a collaborative relationship between human developers and AI systems rather than AI operating independently. This story is notable because it captures a tension playing out across the entertainment and tech industries: companies want the efficiency benefits AI can offer, but they also face pressure from audiences and employees who are wary of AI replacing human creativity and labor. Capcom's public commitment to avoiding AI-generated assets can be seen as an attempt to reassure both players and developers that AI won't erode the artistic identity of its games. At the same time, the scale of change Ishida describes, turning an entire game engine into an AI-centered tool, suggests the company anticipates AI playing an increasingly central role in game production in the years ahead, which could reshape workflows, job responsibilities, and even what skills future game developers need.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Capcom's latest public remarks about artificial intelligence reveal a carefully calibrated strategy that attempts to capture AI's efficiency gains while publicly distancing itself from AI-generated creative content, a tension increasingly common across the entertainment industry. At the Capcom Open Conference RE: 2026, programmer Satoshi Ishida presented on the technical and operational hurdles involved in producing games at the scale and fidelity of the Resident Evil series. He noted that as production values rise, the cumulative time cost of even minor, routine development tasks becomes a serious bottleneck for studios. His proposed remedy was framed in deliberately corporate language: 'successfully integrating AI technology into development workflows,' which refers to the entire pipeline of coding, asset management, testing, and iteration that underlies modern game production. Notably, this framing positions AI as an infrastructural tool rather than a creative author. Capcom has previously made a public commitment not to use AI-generated assets, meaning finished art, character designs, dialogue, or music that reaches players will not be produced by generative AI systems. Ishida's comments largely reinforce that stance, but they also hint at a more expansive trajectory. He described an incremental, long-term plan to transform RE Engine, Capcom's proprietary and widely respected game-development software, into what he called an 'AI-generation game engine.' This phrasing suggests AI capabilities woven directly into the engine's architecture, potentially automating tasks like asset optimization, debugging, or procedural content generation, areas that stop short of final creative output but still represent deep structural change in how games are built. According to a translation from IGN, Ishida articulated an ultimate goal of reaching 'a future where we create games together with AI,' implying a collaborative model in which human developers and AI systems share development responsibilities rather than AI simply assisting at the margins. This announcement matters beyond the gaming industry because it illustrates a broader pattern among technology and creative companies: publicly reassuring audiences and workers that AI won't replace human artistry, while simultaneously investing heavily in AI infrastructure that could substantially reshape labor and workflows over time. Game development is a notoriously labor-intensive and often grueling industry, frequently criticized for demanding excessive overtime from employees, so framing AI as a solution to inefficiency carries genuine appeal for both executives and overworked developers. At the same time, critics of AI adoption across creative industries often worry that incremental integration, starting with 'just' workflow efficiency, can gradually expand into territory that affects creative control, job security, and compensation. Capcom's approach, promising AI involvement in process but not output, represents one attempt to navigate this tension, though whether that distinction holds up as the technology and company plans evolve remains an open question worth watching closely.

questions: How do you think using AI to speed up work, but not to create the actual art or story, changes the way a video game feels compared to one made fully by people?
Do you think it's possible for a company to use AI a little bit now and keep that from growing into using AI a lot more later? Why or why not?
If AI starts helping with more jobs you care about, like making games, art, or even schoolwork, how do you think that could change what jobs look like when you grow up?
